title: Which Tasks Do Transformers Extrapolate To? Now Decidable
hook: Transformers sometimes handle sequences longer than they trained on, sometimes not. For regular languages there's now a complete characterization — and a polynomial-time algorithm to check.
key_points: Before this, it wasn't known which regular languages transformers length-generalize on, despite that being a foundational language class.
The paper gives the first complete characterization, plus a decision algorithm polynomial in the size of the language's syntactic monoid.

Classical Krohn-Rhodes decomposition doesn't apply: its building blocks (flip-flops, simple groups) aren't expressible in C-RASP, and C-RASP's building block (unbounded counting) isn't expressible by finite semigroups.
So length generalization is governed by an algebraic property invisible to classical finite decomposition theory.
The fix is generalizing decomposition theory from finite semigroups to the infinite additive group of the integers, characterizing C-RASP via iterated wreath products of the integers.
Experiments across a broad regular-language suite match transformer behavior more accurately than existing classifications.
content_html: Transformers sometimes generalize to sequences longer than anything they saw in training, and sometimes fall apart immediately. Until now there was no crisp account of which is which — not even for regular languages, the most basic class in formal language theory. Yang, Hahn and colleagues close that gap: they give the first complete characterization of which regular languages transformers length-generalize on, together with a decision algorithm that runs in polynomial time in the size of the language's syntactic monoid.
extra_html:
The route runs through C-RASP, a recently established formalism that expresses which languages transformers length-generalize on; the task becomes characterizing which regular languages live in C-RASP. That turns out to be hard for a specific and interesting reason. The classical tool for decomposing finite semigroups, Krohn-Rhodes theory, doesn't fit from either direction: its atoms — flip-flops and simple groups — aren't expressible in C-RASP, and C-RASP's atom, unbounded counting, isn't expressible by finite semigroups. Length generalization is therefore controlled by an algebraic property that classical finite decomposition theory simply cannot see.

The authors' answer is to generalize decomposition theory from finite semigroups to the infinite additive group on the integers, which lets them characterize C-RASP in terms of iterated wreath products of the integers and extract the polynomial-time decision procedure. Experiments over a broad suite of regular languages match observed transformer length-generalization behavior more accurately than existing classifications. This is theory-heavy work, but the payoff is unusually concrete: for a well-defined family of tasks, "will it extrapolate?" stops being an empirical guess.

related.title: Attention Is All You Need
related.hook: Drop recurrence and convolution, keep only attention — and you get a model that trains in parallel and powers nearly every LLM since.

related.title: Extending Context Windows via Positional Interpolation
related.hook: Don't extrapolate to positions the model never saw - squeeze the position indices back inside the trained range, and a short fine-tune stretches the context window many times over.

related.title: Full-Bandwidth Transformer: Feed the Hidden State Back
related.hook: Between decoding steps a transformer throws away everything except the sampled token. Widening that channel with the top-layer hidden state buys roughly 1.5x the training tokens' worth of quality.

flashcards.prompt: What can you now decide about a regular language, according to this paper?

choices.text: Whether transformers length-generalize on it — in time polynomial in its syntactic monoid
The minimum number of layers a transformer needs to recognize it
Whether a transformer can recognize it at all, at any length

flashcards.explanation_html: The contribution is a complete characterization of length generalization on regular languages plus a polynomial-time decision algorithm — not a bound on recognition or depth.

flashcards.prompt: Why is classical Krohn-Rhodes decomposition theory insufficient here?
flashcards.back_html: Its building blocks — flip-flops and simple groups — aren't expressible in C-RASP, while C-RASP's building block, unbounded counting, isn't expressible by finite semigroups. The two theories miss each other in both directions.

flashcards.prompt: What mathematical move makes the characterization possible?
flashcards.back_html: Generalizing decomposition theory from finite semigroups to the infinite additive group on the integers, which lets C-RASP be characterized in terms of iterated wreath products of the integers.
